Wednesday, 3 May, seven in the morning. Exactly a year ago, Ioana and Julien were getting married at the town hall. Today Hélène turns 86. Rose-Hélène is two months old.
Happy wedding anniversary, Madame Moreau! Breakfast is served in bed, by a loving and slightly exhausted husband.
A year already! When I woke up, I couldn’t believe it. And Rose-Hélène?
She’s asleep, having drunk her whole bottle at five. I’m the one who gave it to her. A tiring night, but a charming daughter.
Did you know that in France the first anniversary is the cotton anniversary? I bought you something made of cotton, for that very reason.
(opens the parcel) A white shirt! And on the pocket, embroidered in blue: "3 May". You’re an amazing woman.
Knowing you’re going to play for Hélène this afternoon, you needed a nice shirt. And you, do you have something for me?
Yes, but you’ll get it tonight. Not having slept, I didn’t have time to wrap it.
Do you know what Hélène told me last Wednesday? That she didn’t want a party, being too old for that.
She told me too. And she asked me, smiling, whether Théo would come and play. She wants a party, believe me.
Right. The residents have prepared a surprise, with Madame Lambert running the operation, of course. Odile is bringing the cake.
Eighty-six candles? We’ll have to call the fire brigade!
(laughs) No, just two candles: an 8 and a 6. And a third, very small one, for Rose-Hélène, who is two months old today.
That’s a touching idea. Hélène will cry. She cries every time she holds her in her arms.
Like you when you listen to Lucia singing. (a cry is heard) Ah… the little princess is awake.
Stay in bed, my love. It’s your day. I’ll go, singing the waltz, as usual.
"-ant" and "-ent" sound the same: the nasal "ahn". "Chantant" = "shahn-tahn", "différent" = "dee-fay-rahn".
"Ay-yahn": the y is read as a short "ee" between the two vowels.
"Ay-tahn", "sa-shahn". The stress falls at the end, as in all French words.
"Ay-moo-vahn": moving. The feminine "émouvante" = "ay-moo-vahnt", the t is heard.
"Noss": the wedding (plural!). "Les noces de coton" = "lay noss duh ko-tohn".

Compound form (earlier action): ayant / étant + past participle. "Ayant bu son biberon, elle dort." = Having drunk her bottle, she’s asleep. "Étant arrivés tôt, ils ont attendu."
2. When to use the present participle
It is mainly a written, elegant form. It has two main roles:
Madame Lambert, who is running the operation…
A candle for Rose-Hélène, who is two months old today.
Knowing you’re going to play, you needed a shirt.
Being too old, she didn’t want a party.

Don’t confuse it with the GERUND (ch. 24): "EN souriant" = while smiling (same person, at the same time). The present participle has no "en" and can describe someone else: "Je vois Hélène souriant." English uses "-ing" for both, hence the confusion.
Many -ant forms are also ADJECTIVES. Then they express a quality and AGREE like any adjective:
des enfants souriant à leur mère
Simple test: if an object follows the form (a noun, "à…"), it’s a participle. If you can put "très" in front, it’s an adjective: "une soirée très charmante".
For a few verbs, the adjective is spelled differently from the participle. They sound the same!
Common mistake: "une nuit fatiguante". Correct: "une nuit FATIGANTE" (adjective, no u).
The unit’s sentence: "Je suis heureuse que vous ayez pu venir, sachant que c’est le jour pour lequel nous avions dit que nous ferions la fête." It contains all four topics.

3 May fell on a Wednesday, which suited everyone: it was the day Julien had been visiting Hélène for almost two years. At three o’clock the little family took the funicular, Julien wearing his new white shirt and Rose-Hélène the blue jumper knitted by the silent gentleman.

The common room was unrecognisable. Madame Lambert, having directed the preparations like a general, had hung balloons everywhere and had the residents write on a big banner: "Happy birthday, Hélène! Happy cotton anniversary, Ioana and Julien!" She had checked the spelling four times.

Hélène was sitting by the window, pretending to read a newspaper. She was wearing her hat from the wedding, the one everyone had admired a year earlier. "I told you I didn’t want a party," she said, smiling, her eyes already shining.

Ioana put Rose-Hélène in her arms. The baby, perhaps smelling the familiar lavender perfume, opened her eyes and looked at her for a long time, very seriously. "She recognises me," Hélène murmured. Nobody dared tell her that at two months it was unlikely.

Then Madame Lambert gave her speech. It lasted twelve minutes, which, for a former schoolteacher, was almost short. Monsieur Petit fell asleep in the middle, snoring softly, and woke up just in time to applaud. He swore he hadn’t missed a thing.

Then Théo sat down at the old piano in the room, a tired instrument, out of tune for years. He was thirteen now, and he had grown a lot. Knowing it was the most important waltz of his life, he had practised every evening for a month.

He played the 1962 waltz, Henri’s waltz, the one that had slept sixty years in a piano. A few notes were out of tune, but nobody noticed. Hélène kept her eyes closed, beating time with one finger on the arm of her chair, like a girl of twenty.

When the last note had faded, Odile Bernard came in, carrying a big chocolate cake. As planned, there were only three candles: an 8, a 6 and a tiny pink one for Rose-Hélène. "One for each generation," Odile explained, a little moved.

Hélène blew out the candles with the baby in her arms. Everyone sang, first in French, then in Spanish thanks to Lucia, then in Romanian thanks to Radu, who sang "La mulți ani" so loudly that Rose-Hélène started to cry. He had to apologise to her for five minutes.

It was then that Radu asked for silence. He had an announcement to make, and he was so nervous that Lucia was holding his hand. "I got a letter this morning," he said. "I’ve been accepted onto the architecture master’s, here in Lyon. I’m staying."

Ioana let out a cry and threw herself into her brother’s arms. Julien gave him a big slap on the back. Lucia, smiling, added that she too had found a job, at an architects’ firm in the Croix-Rousse. She was staying too. The residents applauded without knowing exactly why.

Ioana’s phone rang at that moment: a video call from Iași. Elena and the grandmother appeared on the screen, both dressed as if for a party. They had made a cake too, and they were showing it to the camera, singing.

Hélène took the phone carefully, holding it with both hands, like a fragile object. She looked the grandmother in the eyes, took a deep breath and said, with a terrible but perfectly understandable accent: "Mulțumesc, prietena mea." Radu had taught her those three words in secret.

On the screen, the grandmother put her hand over her mouth. Then she answered something in Romanian, very fast, crying and laughing at the same time. Radu translated: "She says that in August she’ll teach you to dance the hora. And that she won’t accept any excuse."

Before leaving, Hélène asked Julien to open the drawer of her chest of drawers. There was an old yellowed envelope, the one they had found in the piano on moving day. Inside, the original score, handwritten by Henri, with the words: "For Hélène, for her twentieth birthday."

"I’d like to give it to the little one," said Hélène. "Not now, of course. Keep it for her, and give it to her on her twentieth birthday. She carries my name; she may as well carry my waltz." Julien took the envelope without being able to say a word.

In the evening, Odile looked after Rose-Hélène, claiming that a retired paediatrician was the best babysitter in Lyon. Ioana and Julien had dinner at the little Italian restaurant at the bottom of the street, the one where they had celebrated their engagement. The owner remembered them and gave them dessert on the house.

"So, this present you couldn’t wrap?" asked Ioana. Julien smiled mysteriously. "Patience. It can’t be wrapped, and it can’t be given here." They walked home under a pink sky, passing Sophie’s closed bakery.

In the flat, Julien sat down at the piano. He played a waltz Ioana didn’t know, a gentle melody, a little hesitant at first, then more and more joyful. Strange things could be heard in it: a Romanian lullaby, a few notes of flamenco, and even the cry of a baby waking up.

"I wrote it during the nights," Julien explained, "while giving the bottles. Note by note, between three and five in the morning. It’s called Waltz for Two Women." On the score he had written: "For Ioana and Rose-Hélène. Lyon, 3 May 2028."

Ioana said nothing. She looked at the two scores, placed side by side on the piano: Henri’s, yellowed by sixty-six years of waiting, and Julien’s, still white, the ink barely dry. Two waltzes, two men, two women, and one and the same 3 May.

Around eleven, Odile knocked at the door, holding the sleeping Rose-Hélène in her arms, with Victor at her heels. "She was perfect," she whispered. "Victor slept next to the cradle all evening. I think he sees himself as her bodyguard."

Before going to bed, Ioana opened the baby’s diary and wrote, in French, a single line: "3 May. One year of marriage. Two months. Eighty-six years. Three candles, two waltzes, one family." Then she switched off the light, smiling in the dark.

Madame Lambert, the former schoolteacher, has prepared a speech for Hélène’s birthday. Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. At the end you answer 4 questions.
Dear Hélène, dear friends, having been a schoolteacher for forty years, I have never known how to make a short speech. So I ask you for a little patience.
A year ago, Hélène, we saw you leave for the town hall, smiling, in your blue dress. You came back in the evening, exhausted but radiant, having danced all day.
Since then, this house has changed a lot. The workers, working under our windows, wake us every morning. It’s tiring, but it’s also exciting: we are watching a music room being born.
This room will bear the name of a man you loved, Hélène, and who, knowing he would not come back, kept your waltz all his life.
And this year there is a new unofficial resident, a charming little girl who bears your name and who never sleeps during speeches.
So I raise my glass of apple juice, the doctor having forbidden champagne, to your eighty-six years. Happy birthday, Hélène!
